question: A 24-year-old woman presents with oligomenorrhoea, acne, and elevated LH:FSH ratio. You suspect PCOD. Which imaging modality should you choose first, and why?

answers.text: MRI pelvis — it provides the most detail of ovarian morphology without radiation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MRI is not the first-line modality for PCOD. It is costly, not readily available, and adds no diagnostic value over ultrasound for this indication.

answers.text: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) — it directly visualises ovarian morphology and volume at low cost without radiation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. TVS is the recommended first-line modality in Rotterdam criteria. It allows precise follicle counting per ovary and measurement of ovarian volume, which are the two morphological criteria for PCOM.

answers.text: CT pelvis with contrast — it gives cross-sectional detail of both ovaries simultaneously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT involves ionising radiation and offers no advantage over ultrasound for ovarian follicle assessment. It is not indicated for PCOD evaluation.

answers.text: Transabdominal ultrasound alone — it avoids the discomfort of TVS and is adequate for follicle counting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Transabdominal ultrasound is used when TVS is unacceptable (e.g., virgo intacta), but TVS is preferred because it gives superior resolution for small antral follicle counting and accurate ovarian volume measurement.

overallFeedback.feedback: Reconsider — in PCOD, the imaging criterion is polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) assessed by TVS: ≥20 follicles per ovary (2-9 mm each) or ovarian volume >10 mL on either ovary.
TVS is the right answer — it is the standard imaging tool for PCOD evaluation, integrating directly into the Rotterdam criteria without radiation exposure.
